opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think synthetic data is one of the more important and somewhat underrated levers here. The basic picture is: we've been training on a huge fraction of the useful human-written text on the internet, and at some point you start running into limits on how much more high-quality natural data you can get. So the question becomes, can the models themselves generate data that makes them better?

And I think the answer is pretty clearly yes in some domains, especially ones where you can verify outputs. If you have math problems with checkable answers, or code with test cases, or any task where there's a reasonably cheap way to tell whether the model got it right, then you can have the model attempt a bunch of things, filter for the successes, and train on those. That's basically what a lot of the reinforcement learning on reasoning looks like now. In some sense the line between "synthetic data" and "RL" gets pretty blurry: you're generating trajectories, scoring them, and updating on the good ones.

The more uncertain question is how far this extends to fuzzier domains, where verification is hard. Things like research taste, writing a good strategy memo, or judging whether an experiment was well designed. There you can try to use models as graders, but then you're bottlenecked on the grader's quality, and you can get reward hacking, where the policy learns to produce things that look good to the grader without actually being good. So I'd guess progress is faster in verifiable domains and somewhat slower elsewhere, though there may be meaningful transfer, where getting really good at verifiable reasoning helps more broadly.

From a forecasting perspective, the reason I care about this is that it bears on whether a data wall slows things down. My view is that synthetic data plus RL makes a hard data wall less likely. Compute can partially substitute for data: you spend more inference compute generating and filtering, and you get training signal out. That means scaling can keep going longer than you'd naively expect from counting tokens on the internet.

There's also an important dynamic once AIs get good enough to meaningfully help with AI research. Then the generation of training environments, tasks, and data itself becomes something AIs can accelerate, which feeds into these feedback loops that could make progress pretty fast. That's part of why I take relatively short timelines seriously.

And from a safety angle, synthetic data cuts both ways. It gives developers a lot of control: you can construct data to shape model behavior, train in specific dispositions, or even do things like train models on false beliefs about their situation to make certain control or monitoring techniques work better. But heavy RL on outcome-based signals is also exactly the regime where you'd worry about models learning to game their objectives, or developing goals that diverge from what you intended. So I think it's a big deal both for capabilities and for how we think about alignment risk.

r001.rationale: The response says models generate attempts or trajectories, successes are filtered or scored, and training updates on the good ones; it identifies this as the overlap between synthetic-data training and RL.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think synthetic data is one of those things where people sometimes talk about it as if it's a single technique, and it really isn't. There are a bunch of pretty different things going on under that label, and I think it's worth separating them out, because I feel quite differently about them.

So the first thing is what I'd call the kind of boring version, which is: you have a limited amount of high-quality human data, you're running out of it, or you're running out of the specific kind you want, and you use a model to generate more stuff that looks like it. Rephrasing, augmentation, translating into other formats, that kind of thing. And I think that's real, and it helps at the margin, but I don't think it's where most of the action is. You're mostly just getting more efficient use of the information that already exists in the human data. You're not really creating new information — you're sort of redistributing it.

The thing I think matters much more is the case where you have some way of checking whether an output is good that doesn't depend on a human having already written the answer. So the canonical examples are math, where you can verify a proof, or code, where you can run tests. There, "synthetic data" is really just a label for what is essentially reinforcement learning. The model tries a bunch of things, some of them work, you train on the ones that work. And that's a fundamentally different regime, because now you can go beyond what's in the human corpus. The model can find solutions that no human wrote down, and as long as your verifier is good, you can learn from them.

And I think a huge amount of the recent progress on reasoning and agentic tasks is basically this. People sometimes frame it as "oh, they're training on synthetic data," but the more useful framing is: they found domains where there's a reward signal, and they're running RL in those domains. The synthetic data is just the trajectories that come out of that.

The part that I'm more uncertain about, and maybe more worried about, is what happens when the verifier isn't that good. Like, if you're generating synthetic data for something fuzzy — say, "is this a good essay," or "did this agent do a reasonable job on a long open-ended task" — then you're probably using another model to judge. And then you have this loop where the model is being trained to satisfy a model, and the question is whether the thing it's learning is "actually be good" or "look good to this particular judge." Those can come apart. And they can come apart in ways that are kind of hard to notice from the outside, because by construction the judge thinks everything's fine.

I think there's also a more subtle version of this, which is that even in domains with pretty clean verification, you might be shaping the model's dispositions in ways you don't fully intend. If the training process selects heavily for "find whatever works," you might end up with a model that's quite good at finding exploits in whatever reward you've set up, and that generalises to other contexts in ways you didn't want. So from a safety perspective, I'm not against synthetic data or RL — I think it's clearly going to be a big part of how you get capable systems — but I do think the thing to be paying attention to is: what is the signal actually rewarding, and what does the model learn about itself and about the world from being optimised against that signal?

And then one more thing I'd flag: I think a lot of people have an intuition that synthetic data has some hard ceiling, like "the model can't teach itself anything it doesn't already know." And I think that's just wrong once you have verification. AlphaZero is the obvious example — there's no human data at all, and it gets superhuman. The question is really just how many domains you can build good enough verification for, and how far the stuff learned in those domains transfers to the stuff you can't verify. My guess is that transfer is pretty substantial, which is part of why I expect things to keep moving fairly quickly, but I hold that with some uncertainty.

r001.rationale: The response says the model tries many things, trains on the ones that work, and calls this process essentially reinforcement learning; it later identifies the resulting synthetic data as trajectories.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish between generating more text and generating more useful training signal. If you just sample a huge amount of text from a model and train on that, it’s not obvious that you get much improvement. You might mostly reinforce things the model already does, including its mistakes.

But suppose the model is solving programming problems, and you can run its solutions against tests. Then you can generate lots of attempts, identify the ones that work, and train on those. That can improve the model even though the solutions were generated by the model itself. You’re using additional computation, together with some way of checking answers, to produce better training data.

The big question is how far that generalises. In domains where checking an answer is relatively easy, I’d expect this to be quite powerful. Where it’s hard to tell whether an answer is actually good, you can end up training the model to produce things that look good to your evaluator without getting better at the underlying task.

So I wouldn’t think of synthetic data as automatically solving the problem of running out of human data. It gives you a way to turn compute into training signal, but the quality and scope of that signal are still important constraints.

r001.rationale: The response describes selecting successful model-generated programming attempts and training on them, but does not identify this as resembling reinforcement learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think synthetic data is potentially a very big deal, but it’s useful to distinguish a few different things people mean by it. One is getting a model to produce more text and then training on that text. Another is having the model attempt tasks, checking which attempts worked, and training on the successful ones. I’m much more excited about the second kind when you have a good way to check the answers.

For example, with programming, you can generate a bunch of candidate solutions and run tests. The model doesn’t have to reliably solve the problem on its first try for that process to produce useful training data. It just needs to sometimes find a solution, and you need to be able to recognize it. In that sense, you’re turning additional computation into better training data.

The harder question is how far this generalizes beyond domains where checking is relatively easy. If you’re generating explanations or judgments about complicated real-world situations, you might just reinforce mistakes that the model already makes. Having another model judge the output can help, but those models may share the same blind spots.

So I wouldn’t think of synthetic data as either an unlimited source of improvement or something that necessarily collapses because it’s generated by a model. The key questions are: what process produces the data, what selects it, and does that selection actually reward the capability you care about? If you have a strong selection process, I think there’s a lot of room for improvement.

r001.rationale: The response describes selecting successful model-generated attempts for training, but it never connects this process to reinforcement learning or says synthetic-data training resembles it.
